blocks.etymology: Possibly from a dialectal form *swiden of Middle English swithen, past participle of Middle English swithen (“to burn, scorch, singe”), from Old Norse svíða (“to singe, burn”). Compare also Old Norse sviðinn (“burnt, singed”, past participle). Alternatively, from Old Norse sviðna (“to be burned”) or Old High German swedan (“to be burned”). Either way, probably ultimately from Proto-Germanic *swīþaną. First attested in 1868. If their respective theories align, then a distant cognate of German Schwyz, hence Swiss.

wiktionary.gloss: An area of land that has been cleared by cutting the vegetation and burning it; slash and burn.

blocks.etymology: From thirteen + -er (suffix denoting people characterized by something, or people or things to which certain measurements or numbers apply).

wiktionary.gloss: A child who is thirteen years old.
A member of the 13th Gen; a Generation Xer or Gen-Xer.
The last playing card of a suit left after the other twelve have been played.
A hit for thirteen runs.
A coin worth thirteenpence, especially an Irish shilling (as contrasted with a British shilling which was worth twelvepence).
A thirteen-syllable line or series of lines in a poem.
A mountain rising to more than 13,000 feet (about 4,000 metres) but less than 14,000 feet above mean sea level.
To put oneself in a difficult situation.
To become anxious or upset; to fret.

blocks.etymology: Calque of Latin sub rosā.

examples: We are organising (but this is quite under the rose as yet) a company for the production of furniture and decoration of all kinds, for the sale of which we are going to open an actual shop!

blocks.etymology: From Middle English unfeithful, equivalent to un- + faithful.
